questions.answer: A \(1\times 1\) determinant is the single entry itself. The matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}4\end{pmatrix}\) has only entry 4. Therefore \(\det\left(\begin{pmatrix}4\end{pmatrix}\right)\) = 4.

For \(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\), the determinant is ad - bc. Here \(a=2\), \(b=3\), \(c=5\), and \(d=7\). Compute \(2\cdot7\) - \(3\cdot5\) = 14 - 15 = -1. Therefore the determinant is -1.
Use ad - bc. Here \(a=1\), \(b=-4\), \(c=2\), and \(d=3\). The determinant is \(1\cdot3\) - (-4)*2 = 3 + 8 = 11. Therefore \(\det\left(\begin{pmatrix}1&-4\\2&3\end{pmatrix}\right)\) = 11.

questions.prompt: Find all real t such that \(\det\left(\begin{pmatrix}t&1\\3&2\end{pmatrix}\right)\) = 5.
questions.answer: Use the \(2\times 2\) determinant formula. \(\det\left(\begin{pmatrix}t&1\\3&2\end{pmatrix}\right)\) = 2t - 3. Set this equal to 5: 2t - 3 = 5. Add 3 to get 2t = 8, so \(t=4\). Therefore \(t=4\).
This matrix is diagonal. The determinant of a triangular or diagonal matrix is the product of its diagonal entries. Therefore the determinant is \(1\cdot2\)*3 = 6.
The matrix is upper triangular because all entries below the main diagonal are zero. The determinant is the product of the diagonal entries: \(2\cdot3\)*(-1) = -6. Therefore the determinant is -6.
This is an upper triangular matrix, so its determinant is the product of the diagonal entries. The diagonal entries are 1, 4, and 6. Therefore \(\\det=1\)*\(4\cdot6\) = 24.

questions.prompt: Compute \(\det\left(\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\0&1&4\\5&6&0\end{pmatrix}\right)\) using expansion along the first row.
questions.answer: Expand along the first row: \(\\det=1\)*\(\det\left(\begin{pmatrix}1&4\\6&0\end{pmatrix}\right)\) - \(2\cdot \det\left(\begin{pmatrix}0&4\\5&0\end{pmatrix}\right)\) + \(3\cdot \det\left(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\5&6\end{pmatrix}\right)\). Compute the minors: \(1\cdot0\) - \(4\cdot6\) = -24, \(0\cdot0\) - \(4\cdot5\) = -20, and \(0\cdot6\) - \(1\cdot5\) = -5. Therefore \(\\det=1\)*(-24) - 2*(-20) + 3*(-5) = -24 + 40 - 15 = 1.

questions.prompt: Compute \(\det\left(\begin{pmatrix}2&0&1\\3&0&4\\5&1&6\end{pmatrix}\right)\) by expanding along the second column.
questions.answer: The second column is \((0,0,1)\), so expanding along it is efficient. Only the entry in row 3 column 2 contributes. Its sign is negative because (-1)^(3+2) = -1. The minor is \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\), whose determinant is \(2\cdot4\) - \(1\cdot3\) = 5. Therefore \(\\det=1\)*(-1)*5 = -5.

questions.prompt: A learner computes \(\det\left(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\right)\) as \(1\cdot4\) + \(2\cdot3\) = 10. Diagnose the error and give the correct determinant.
questions.answer: The learner added the two diagonal products, but the \(2\times 2\) determinant uses ad - bc, not ad + bc. Here \(a=1\), \(b=2\), \(c=3\), \(d=4\). The correct determinant is \(1\cdot4\) - \(2\cdot3\) = 4 - 6 = -2.
